subject: Cloud Computing
title: OpenStack: The Open Cloud Dream
description: One-minute skill: OpenStack: The Open Cloud Dream.

hook.text: In 2010, NASA and Rackspace released free software so anyone could build their own cloud.

buildup.text: OpenStack promised to break AWS lock-in. Companies could run cloud infrastructure themselves.

discovery.text: Major companies joined in: IBM, HP, Intel, and dozens more funded its development.

twist.text: But OpenStack was fiendishly complex. Most companies found it cheaper to just pay AWS.

climax.text: OpenStack didn't kill AWS. But it proved the demand for cloud alternatives was real.

punchline.text: Open source clouds are free. Until you count the labor.

quiz.question: Why did OpenStack fail to dethrone AWS?
options: It was too complex for most companies to operate themselves
AWS bought OpenStack and shut it down
OpenStack could only run on specialized hardware

details.summary: OpenStack launched in 2010 as an open-source alternative to AWS, letting organizations build their own private clouds. While it gained significant adoption, its complexity limited its appeal, and many organizations eventually chose public cloud providers instead.
details.whyItMatters: OpenStack proved that building your own cloud is technically possible but operationally challenging. Its story illustrates why most organizations choose public clouds over building their own.
takeaways: OpenStack let organizations build private clouds with open-source tools
Many OpenStack users eventually migrated to public clouds

faq.question: Why was OpenStack created?
faq.answer: Rackspace and NASA collaborated to create an open-source cloud platform that would prevent vendor lock-in to AWS. OpenStack offered compute, storage, and networking components that organizations could assemble into a private cloud running in their own data centers.

faq.question: What happened to OpenStack?
faq.answer: OpenStack remains in use at large organizations and telecom companies that need custom private clouds. However, many smaller adopters abandoned it due to operational complexity. The project continues under the Open Infrastructure Foundation with a more focused scope.
